facts.claim: Higher intake of ultra-processed foods is linked to reduced grip strength, slower gait speed, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) and lower muscle mass indices (MMI, AMMI).
facts.quote: A dose-dependent relationship was evident, with higher UPF intake linked to reduced grip strength, slower gait speed, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) and lower muscle mass indices (MMI, AMMI).

facts.claim: Dietary patterns rich in ultra-processed foods may contribute to low-grade systemic inflammation and early metabolic dysfunction in children and adolescents.
facts.quote: Emerging evidence suggests that dietary patterns rich in UPF may contribute to low-grade systemic inflammation and early metabolic dysfunction in children and adolescents.

facts.claim: High ultra-processed food intake is linked to higher levels of liver biomarkers related to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in older adults with overweight/obesity and metabolic syndrome.
facts.quote: In multivariable models, each 10% daily increment in UPF consumption in 1 year was associated with significantly greater FLI (β 1. 60 points, 95% CI 1. 24;1. 96 points) and HSI (0. 43, 0. 29; 0. 57) scores (all p-values < 0. 001).

facts.claim: Most of the latest findings have revealed an adverse impact of high ultra-processed food consumption on metabolic health, including cardiovascular diseases and mortality.
facts.quote: Most of the latest findings have revealed an adverse impact of high UPF consumption on metabolic health, including cardiovascular diseases and mortality.

facts.claim: No study reported an association between ultra-processed foods and beneficial health outcomes.
facts.quote: No study reported an association between UPF and beneficial health outcomes.

research.angle: Ultra-processed foods are linked to systemic inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and adverse health outcomes across various life stages, including children and older adults.
research.verdict: The evidence consistently links high ultra-processed food consumption to metabolic issues and inflammation, though many studies are observational and require further research to confirm causality.
research.caveat: Direct evidence on ultra-processed food consumption remains limited, and many findings rely on indirect evidence or observational studies.
